messages.author: 395fec07c2012bfa
messages.subject: MSStatsTMT adjusted p value
parts:
Dear MSstats Team,

I am analyzing a TMT10plex dataset with MSStatsTMT, generated from ProteomeDiscoverer. However, I get same adjusted pvalue on many occasions and none of the proteins have adjusted p< 0.05, however around 600 proteins with p<0.05 in a dataset of 8000 proteins (for one of the comparisons). Is there anything wrong with the scripts below? I am comparing 3 conditions and doing 'pairwise comparison, I have compared with individual 'contrasts' (not pairwise); the result is the same.

input.pd <- PDtoMSstatsTMTFormat(input = raw.pd, annotation = annotation)

quant.pd.msstats <- proteinSummarization(input.pd,
                                         method="msstats",
                                         global_norm=TRUE,
                                         reference_norm=FALSE,
                                         remove_norm_channel = TRUE,
                                         remove_empty_channel = TRUE)

test.pd.pairwise <- groupComparisonTMT(data = quant.pd.msstats, 
                                   contrast.matrix = "pairwise",
                                   moderated = TRUE, 
                                   adj.method = "BH",
                                   save_fitted_models = TRUE,
                                   use_log_file = TRUE,
                                   verbose = TRUE)

Kind regards,
Sudip

Hi Sudip,

According to the testing results you shared, there are no significant proteins because (1) the standard error is large; (2) the sample size is small. 

I would recommend looking at the profile plot using function dataProcessPlotsTMT() to figure out why the standard error is large. The function may take a while since it generates a profile plot for each protein.

Best,
Ting

messages.author: 2889aa2e61425c8e
messages.subject: Re: MSStatsTMT adjusted p value
parts:
Hi Sudip,

You must use adjusted p-values if you'd like to make any claims of statistical significance (including error rate control etc).

If you only want to rank protein candidates for a subsequent followup, while ignoring statistical significance, you can use raw p-values. But please keep in mind that this ranking may be unreliable, and can lead to irreproducible results.

Thank you for using MSstats
Sincerely
Olga

messages.subject: Re: MSStatsTMT adjusted p value
parts:
You should use adjusted p-values instead of the original p-values. The adjustment accounts for the fact that you do tests for many proteins. As far as the adjusted p-value cutoff, standard values are 0.01, 0.05 and 0.1. All of them are fine, as long as you choose the cutoff before you have seen the data

Sincerely
OV
